newsitem.title: USA: White House, Republicans agree on U.S. tax cut plan.
newsitem.headline: White House, Republicans agree on U.S. tax cut plan.

text.p: Congressional Republicans and the White House agreed on Monday to a tax cut package that was bigger than what they first bargained for -- expected to amount to more than $90 billion over five years.
If approved by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton it would be the first major American tax cut in 16 years.

"We have exceeded the goal of $85 billion in net tax cuts," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said. That goal was set in the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House.
"It's a much stronger tax bill than most people thought we could get," House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said.
In announcing the "tentative agreement," Republicans and the White House did not give out specific details, which were expected on Tuesday.

In general, the White House bargained for provisions that gave more tax breaks to low-income individuals than Republican plans. And the Republicans got their way on their high-priority items such as a capital gains tax cut and inheritance tax relief.
The biggest piece is a $500-per-child tax credit, expected to cost about $85 billion, which would be more than originally proposed in either the Senate or House bills.
The White House agreed to give the child credit to upper-middle-income families, with the amount phasing out starting at incomes of $110,000.

The Republicans gave ground to allow more low-income working families to be eligible, starting at incomes of $18,000, a congressional aide said. The administration agreed to $5 billion in savings from tightening compliance on the earned-income tax credit for the working poor.
Tax breaks for higher education were expected to total about $40 billion over five years and include President Clinton's HOPE scholarship which is a $1,500 tax credit for college education costs.

A key victory for Republicans was a long-sought capital gains tax cut. The White House won on its objection to a provision that would not tax profits due to inflation, called "indexing," which was eliminated from the tax package.

The maximum tax rate on investment profits would be cut to 20 percent from 28 percent. But investors who made profits on an asset sold between May 7 and July 28 would have had to own it for the previous 12 months to receive the 20 percent rate. Investors who sell an asset on July 29 or later would have to have owned it for 18 months to receive that lower rate.
Shorter-term investment gains are considered ordinary income and would be taxed at the investor's income tax rate.

A new long-term capital gains tax measure was added to the legislation. It would give investors an even-lower 18 percent rate for profits on investments bought in 2001 and held for more than five years, congressional aides said.

Aviation taxes and fees were expected to account for the bulk of the roughly $50 billion in revenue increases. The legislation would lower the 10 percent airline ticket tax to 7.5 percent over three years, a congressional aide said. A $12 international arrival and departure fee would be imposed on passengers, who now only pay a $6 departure fee.
Republicans were already talking about more tax cuts in the years ahead. "We see this as a launching point for an even better next couple of years," Gingrich said.

The administration agreed to greater inheritance tax relief than even the Republicans had originally proposed. The threshold at which the estate tax kicks in would be raised to $1.3 million immediately from $600,000 for small farms and businesses. Estate tax relief for individuals would be phased in over a number of years to a $1 million threshold.

Expanded Individual Retirement Accounts would also be in the tax bill, including a provision allowing a non-working spouse to contribute $2,000 annually to a retirement IRA and allow penalty-free withdrawal for first-time home purchase.
The ethanol subsidy would expire at the end of 2000 as the current law states. Some lawmakers had been pushing for an extension at a reduced level after the expiry.
